newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Midwest governors mull electric deregulation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Midwest governors mull electric deregulation.

text.p: Commercial electric customers will be active participants in the spot market as the electric industry is deregulated, an industry observer said Monday during the Midwestern Governors' Conference.

William Hogan, conference keynote speaker and professor of public policy and management at Harvard University, said the most likely result of deregulation will be commercial customers' use of spot market contracts to hedge against fluctuating prices.
Hogan said the effects of deregulation on residential customers would be more subdued.

He said residential customers would likely buy electricity under deregulation in the same way they currently buy fuel for cars and trucks. Specifically, he said, there will be no contracting as there will be for commercial customers.
The two-day conference, hosted by Kansas Gov. Bill Graves, was considering electric and telecommunication deregulation.

Kansas and other states are studying proposals to deregulate the electric industry through a system called retail wheeling, in which consumers would choose their electric company in much the same way as they now choose a long-distance telephone carrier.

Hogan cast doubt on what he called the "old model" of retail wheeling, which envisioned customers physically detaching themselves from a local utility to purchase power from a different supplier that uses different generating units.

Hogan said customers will remain attached to the same wires over which power flows, and that the flow of power will not change if the market is efficient. As a result, retail wheeling represents a financial transaction and not a physical change, Hogan said.
"In the context of a competitive market, the old model of retail wheeling is revealed as a fiction," Hogan said in prepared remarks he distributed to reporters.
Participants in a panel discussion about electric industry deregulation said changes will not just affect the utilities themselves but may also touch shareholders and residential customers.
Deregulation could result in higher rates for residential customers, depending on whether utility customers are required to share the cost of utilities' idle or inefficient assets, the panel said.

Western Resouces Chairman and Chief Executive John Hayes, a panel participant, warned against the impact of deregulation on utility shareholders. If investor-owned utilies are hurt by deregulation, their shareholders -- mainly retirees or so-called "widows and orphans" -- may suffer, Hayes said.

Deregulation could also lead to rate wars among publicly held utilities that could put non-profit utilities at a disadvantage, said Wiliam Mayben, president and chief executive of the Nebraska Public Power District, a power provider to rural areas.
The Midwestern Governors' Conference is made up of the governors of Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota and Wisconsin.
